name: video
description: A video as a static, PDF-safe embed: a poster that links to the clip, a play badge, the provider's name, and a scannable QR to the same URL — never a live iframe.
purpose: Use to put a YouTube / Vimeo / TikTok / Instagram video on a slide. Because the deck renders to a static PDF (and the engine bars iframes), a `video` slide shows a POSTER with a play badge + provider label — the poster is a clickable link in the HTML/PDF — and, when you add the `qr` modifier, a scannable code the room can scan to watch. Two compositions: `companion` (a claim leads on the left, the clip proves it on the right) and `gallery` (a contained, matted exhibit). Author the clip as one `@video{"https://…", title="…", poster=…}` record on a line of its own (the video plugin draws it); the provider is auto-detected.

heading.description: Optional heading — the so-what of the clip, not 'Video'.

video.description: The clip, written as a `@video{"https://…"}` record on a line of its own. The video plugin draws the poster, play badge and provider label from that record; the layout adds the QR on a `qr` slide.

caption.description: Optional: the record's `title="…"`, shown under the poster.

## The video card plays beside its context.

Ninety seconds, unscripted: signup to a published deck without touching support.

`@video{"https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aqz-KE-bpKQ", title="Ree A., Head of Ops at Northwind"}`

whenToUse.title: A clip makes the point better than a screenshot
whenToUse.body: A product walkthrough, a customer testimonial, a demo reel — anywhere motion carries the argument. The slide shows a clean poster; the room scans the QR (or clicks it in the HTML/PDF) to watch.

whenToUse.title: The URL is all you have to write
whenToUse.body: Write the YouTube / Vimeo / TikTok / Instagram link in one `@video{…}` record; the provider is detected and the QR is generated for you. Add `poster=…` only when you want a specific still (required for Instagram, whose thumbnails aren't fetchable).

whenToUse.title: Closing / hand-off slides
whenToUse.body: A 'watch the full demo' or 'see the launch film' send-off pairs a poster with a scannable code the audience takes with them — the same pattern as the QR closing/divider variants.

antiPatterns.title: Expecting it to autoplay in the PDF
antiPatterns.body: A PDF is paper — it can't play video, and the engine bars iframes for security. `video` is a poster + scannable link by design. If you need in-app playback, that's a separate interactive surface, not a boardroom deck.

antiPatterns.title: A wall of caption
antiPatterns.body: The caption is one line — 'Scan to watch', a title, a runtime. If you're writing a paragraph about the video, put it in a `content` slide and drop the clip in as a supporting `video`.

antiPatterns.title: Instagram with no poster
antiPatterns.body: Instagram's public thumbnails aren't fetchable, so an Instagram `video` with no `poster=` word falls back to a plain placeholder tile. Author a `poster` for a real still.

related.name: image
related.when: the visual is a still photo or screenshot, not a video

related.name: closing
related.when: the send-off is a call to action with a QR, not a specific clip

related.name: diagram
related.when: the motion you want is an animated process — a Mermaid diagram may say it statically

commonMistakes.mistake: The clip is still a bare bullet, with `caption` and `poster` bullets beside it.
commonMistakes.fix: The bullet form is gone: the address comes only from your own `@video{…}` record, never from slide text. `lint:deck --fix` rewrites the bullets into the record (`video-bullet`).

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing a second `@video{…}` expecting a second clip or a contact-sheet grid.
commonMistakes.fix: The layout seats one clip; the first record on the slide is the one it lays out.
Quote it: `@video{"https://youtu.be/x?t=90"}`. Segno names the fix.

variantDecisionRule.useWhen: A standalone video callout with no strong claim beside it — poster plus meta column, the simplest look.
A specific claim leads the slide and the clip proves it — text and poster split left/right.
The video is more exhibit than pitch — contained on a matte the way a diagram or screenshot would be.
The room should be able to open the clip on their own phones — combines with any other variant to add a scannable code beside the poster.

venueCapacity.none: The poster fills its box and scales, so no element count marks where it stops fitting.
